Allpowers Volix P300 Review: Efficiency and Limits - Best Batteries 
 Allpowers Volix P300: Our Full Review
 Author: Julien De Jurquet 
 Review published on September 6, 2026 at 10:38 · 11 min read 
 213 Wh actually delivered out of the claimed 256 Wh through the AC outlet, but up to 241 Wh through the 12V output: the gap comes down to the inverter's own power draw, and it sums up what matters most before choosing the Allpowers Volix P300.
 Our rating
 4.1 /5 
 How is this rating calculated? 
 The essentials
 The Allpowers Volix P300 delivers on real portability: 7.9 lb (3.57 kg) for 256 Wh, a clear screen, and a full app with Bluetooth and WiFi, a rare combination at this size and price. Its AC outlet delivers around 213 Wh out of the claimed 256 Wh (83%), rising to 241 Wh through the 12V output, the gap coming down to the inverter's own power draw. Two real drawbacks hold it back: a full AC charge takes closer to 82 minutes than the advertised hour, and a solar undervoltage fault along with a restart that isn't always automatic after a long outage are worth knowing about before relying on it for unattended backup. No safety incident is on record for this model, but a couple of commercial details (the real cycle threshold, the warranty length) are worth checking directly with the seller. A genuinely honest, well-equipped little station for camping, occasional remote work or light home backup, less suited to a long, fully unattended backup role.
 Strengths
 Very light for its class (7.9 lb / 3.57 kg) with full control: screen, Bluetooth AND WiFi, dedicated app
 The USB-C port beats its own spec: 105W delivered against a 100W claim, with PPS support
 Highly efficient 12V and USB-C outputs: up to 94% and over 90% of rated capacity delivered
 Fast UPS switchover, around 16ms in both directions, quicker than the claimed 20ms
 Meets standard lithium safety and transport certification (UN38.3), with no safety incident on record so far
 Limitations
 Full AC charge slower than advertised: around 82 minutes instead of one hour
 Efficiency collapses on a light, continuous AC load: barely 17% at 3W over more than fifteen hours
 A solar undervoltage fault (E302) blocks charging at dusk until the panel is manually unplugged and replugged
 Restart isn't always automatic after a long AC outage, worth checking before any unattended backup role
 The real cycle threshold sits at 70% capacity per the manual, against the 80% the spec sheet implies
 The fan runs in short, not always smooth cycles, more noticeable than an 'ultra-quiet' label suggests

 In summary
 The Allpowers Volix P300 delivers around 213 Wh out of the claimed 256 Wh through its AC outlet, and up to 241 Wh through its 12V output.
 The USB-C port beats its own spec: up to 105W delivered against a 100W claim, with PPS support.
 A full AC charge takes around 82 minutes at maximum power, against the one hour claimed by the manufacturer.
 The UPS switchover sits around 16ms in both directions, quicker than the claimed 20ms.
 On a light, continuous 3W load, barely 45 Wh out of the claimed 256 Wh remain usable before shutdown.
 The official manual sets the threshold for the claimed 4000 charge cycles at 70% remaining capacity, not the 80% the spec sheet implies.

 What the claimed 256 Wh are actually worth
 The Volix P300 packs a 256 Wh LiFePO4 battery (12.8V, 20Ah), rated for over 4000 charge cycles. That label figure says nothing about what actually comes out of the ports, though, and the gap depends heavily on which output is used.

 Through the AC outlet, at 150W (roughly a power-hungry laptop or a small multi-device charger), the station delivers around 213 Wh, or 83% of its rated capacity. The difference comes down to DC/AC conversion: the inverter draws a fixed amount of power to run, regardless of what's plugged in.
 That conversion doesn't exist on the DC outputs. The 12V output delivers up to 241 Wh, or 94% of the rated figure, and the USB-C port tops 90% at 60W. Charging a phone, tablet or USB-C laptop therefore pulls noticeably more usable energy out of the Volix P300 than the AC outlet does.
 Out of the claimed 256 Wh, how much actually stays usable depends heavily on the output and the power drawn. The gap becomes dramatic on a very light, continuous load: at just 3W, the level of a router or a small home gateway, barely 45 Wh out of the claimed 256 Wh remain usable before shutdown, or barely 17%, over more than fifteen hours. Most of the energy is absorbed by the inverter's own baseline power draw rather than by whatever is plugged in. This isn't unique to the Volix P300: it's a physical trait of every small inverter-based station, the lighter and longer the load, the worse the efficiency.
 The practical takeaway: the Volix P300 is a strong choice for short, meaningful loads (charging a laptop, a camera, running a small appliance for a few dozen minutes), and a much weaker one for keeping a very low-draw device running continuously off its AC outlet for hours.
 300W continuous, 600W peak: power delivery that holds its promise
 The spec sheet claims 300W continuous and 600W peak on the single AC outlet. Both figures hold up under everyday loads (a laptop, a small multi-device charger, a fan, lighting), with no thermal throttling or shortfall against the claimed output. Housing temperature stays at or under 109 °F (43 °C) around the vents under a 150W AC load, with no sign of overheating.
 The USB-C port actually beats its own promise: up to 105W available against the 100W claim, with PPS support alongside standard PD across six voltage profiles. Enough to fast-charge a recent laptop or a flagship phone at full speed, matching a dedicated AC charger.
 The Volix P300's real limit isn't power, then, it's provisioning: a single AC outlet. At this capacity tier (256 Wh), that's the class norm rather than a shortfall specific to this unit (most comparable stations only offer one too), but it does rule out running several AC-powered devices at once. The outlet itself sits rotated 90° relative to the housing, a choice that makes room for bulky power bricks without them overhanging the other ports.
 The one-hour full charge promise, and what it actually takes
 The manufacturer claims a full 0-100% AC charge in one hour at the maximum 300W input. A partial charge to 80% in 40 minutes lines up with that claim. The rest doesn't: a full charge actually takes closer to 82 minutes, the final stretch slowing down noticeably as it nears 100%, as with nearly all lithium batteries.
 The final stretch of the charge (80 to 100%) slows down noticeably, pushing a full charge to 82 minutes rather than the advertised hour. The app offers several charging modes (fast, normal, quiet), adjusting input power between roughly 90W and 290W. The slowest mode isn't fully silent either: the fan keeps running, which, combined with the longer charge time, actually makes it slightly less efficient than the fast mode.
 On solar, the XT60 input accepts up to 110W (11-30V). At close to maximum power (around 108W), a full charge takes just over three hours; at lower power (around 68W), nearly four and a half hours. Combined AC-and-solar charging works normally, letting both sources add up for a faster top-up.
 Worth knowing before an unattended solar charge: an undervoltage fault (coded E302) can trigger at dusk, as panel voltage drops with the fading light. Rather than resuming on its own once voltage recovers, the station latches the fault and blocks charging until the solar connector is unplugged and replugged.
 UPS backup: a fast switchover, but not always a clean restart
 The Volix P300 includes a UPS function: on an AC power outage, it switches to its own battery to keep a sensitive device running (a desktop computer, a home gateway, a small home network). The manufacturer claims a 20ms switchover. In both directions, AC-to-battery and then battery-to-AC once power returns, the switchover actually sits closer to 16ms, slightly better than claimed.

 One detail is worth knowing before trusting the station with a critical, unattended backup role: as AC power returns, output voltage briefly runs through an unstable waveform before settling, and a full restart after a long outage isn't always automatic. For a brief outage behind a computer or a gateway, the fast switchover is more than enough to prevent data loss. For a long, unattended home-backup role, it's worth checking the wake-up behavior yourself before making it your only line of defense.
 Left plugged in permanently for this role, the Volix P300 draws very little power: around 3W on simple AC standby, up to 5W with the UPS function kept active continuously. Over a year, that draw is negligible next to the cost of an unprotected outage.
 Ports and app control: a complete package for its size
 For a 256 Wh station, the port selection is complete: one AC outlet, two USB-A ports (18W each), a USB-C port up to 105W, a 12V car-style output (120W, with a rubber cap) and the XT60 solar input. That lineup matches what direct competitors of similar capacity offer, no more, no less.
 What sets the Volix P300 apart in its class is control: a local LCD screen, Bluetooth AND WiFi, and a full app to track charge level, adjust charging power or trigger the UPS function remotely. Several direct competitors of similar capacity are limited to Bluetooth only, or skip an app entirely. That control layer isn't flawless, though: early on, the Bluetooth connection had to be manually re-enabled at every power-up, a friction point since fixed through an app update.
 The housing itself stays very compact: 10.2 x 8.3 x 4.9 in (26 x 21 x 12.5 cm) for 7.9 lb (3.57 kg), roughly the size of a large 2-liter bottle, small enough to tuck under a monitor or into a camera bag without getting in the way.
 Fan noise, warranty and build: what's known and what isn't
 The manufacturer claims a 30dB noise level under load, described as comparable to a light breeze. That figure hasn't been independently confirmed to date. The fan's behavior is better documented, though: it kicks in through short, not always smooth cycles as soon as the AC output or fast charging is active, more noticeable in practice than an "ultra-quiet" label suggests. Even the slowest charging mode doesn't fully silence the fan.
 No teardown has turned up to identify the cell brand or BMS details, so that information stays out of this review rather than being guessed at.
 Two details worth checking before buying: the official manual sets the threshold for the claimed 4000 charge cycles at 70% remaining capacity, while the spec sheet implies 80%, a less generous baseline than it first appears next to competitors quoting their own cycle counts at 80%. And on warranty, the brand's official site claims 5 years, while some documentation and resellers list only 2: worth clarifying directly with the seller at purchase.
 On substance, no safety incident or recurring hardware fault is on record for this model to date: the drawbacks covered here concern software, ergonomics and commercial documentation, not the build itself.
 Against the direct competition and the rest of the Allpowers lineup
 In its capacity tier (250-290 Wh, 300W), several direct competitors already sit in the catalog. The table below lines them up on the criteria that compare most directly.
 Comparison with directly comparable stations (250-290 Wh, 300W) Model Capacity Continuous power Weight Real-world output

 Against these figures, the Volix P300 sits mid-pack on real-world AC output, clearly ahead on the 12V output, and among the best equipped for control: Bluetooth and WiFi combined, where several competitors settle for Bluetooth only or skip an app altogether. It does charge more slowly than the EcoFlow River 2 (a proven 60 minutes) and the River 3 (57 minutes), which remain the benchmarks for AC charge speed at this size.
 Against the Allpowers S300 Plus, a larger sibling (288 Wh against 256 Wh) sold in a neighboring range from the same brand, the Volix P300 sticks with standard LiFePO4 chemistry rather than its sibling's NMC cells, and a spec sheet with no identified contradiction across its own official documents.
 Reliability, software updates and warranty
 Allpowers is now a well-represented brand in this comparison, with several other stations across different ranges already in the catalog. No product recall or safety alert is on record for the Volix P300 to date.
 The one documented software bug, a Bluetooth connection needing to be re-paired at every power-up, has since been fixed through an app update, a sign of active software support. The two faults mentioned above (the E302 solar undervoltage lock, and error code E209 missing from the manual) remain unresolved to date, however.
 Technical support runs through the manufacturer's contact address. As with any recent release, there isn't yet enough track record to judge 5- or 10-year reliability. The claimed 4000 cycles, applied to a full charge every two days, work out to more than 20 years of use in theory: a useful order of magnitude to keep in mind, not a promise proven over time.
 Camping, remote work, photo or backup: where it truly fits
 At 7.9 lb (3.57 kg) and a compact footprint, it makes a credible camping companion: it powers lighting, charges phones and cameras, runs a small fan, and recharges in just over an hour on AC power before heading out again. Rated for discharge from 14 °F to 104 °F (-10 °C to 40 °C), it tolerates cool outings, but charging needs to stay between 32 °F and 104 °F (0 °C to 40 °C). Large kitchen appliances (a kettle, a hot plate, an oven) stay out of reach of its 300W, an accepted limit of this size class.
 For occasional remote work, it powers a laptop and a mobile hotspot for several hours, with a comfortable margin thanks to its 100W USB-C port that can fast-charge a second device at the same time. Its UPS function guards a workstation against micro-outages, with the caveats already covered for a long, unattended backup role.
 For photo or video work in the field, its 256 Wh recharge several mirrorless camera batteries, a drone pack or mics, and its USB-C output runs a fill LED panel between takes. Its featherweight build makes it a discreet backup to slip into a camera bag.
 On a road trip or in a van, charging from the vehicle's 12V outlet is the most efficient of the three input paths for topping up available energy, with the 110W solar option useful but slower, and the E302 lockout at dusk worth knowing about before relying on it unattended.
 Who the Volix P300 suits, and who it doesn't
 The Volix P300 suits anyone after a light energy reserve with complete control (screen, Bluetooth, WiFi, app) at an affordable price, for camping, occasional remote work, nomadic photo work or a first line of defense against home micro-outages. Its highly efficient 12V and USB-C outputs also make it a good pick for anyone mostly charging DC devices rather than AC-powered gear.
 It suits fewer people looking to run a router or a home gateway continuously off its AC outlet for hours on end, since efficiency collapses on that kind of light, sustained load, anyone after the fastest possible AC charge in its class (the EcoFlow River 2 or River 3 do better on that specific point), or anyone wanting to hand over a long, fully unattended home-backup role without ever checking its wake-up behavior.
 Taken for what it is rather than what it doesn't claim to be, the Volix P300 remains an honest little station: it delivers on its power and weight promises, beats its own USB-C spec, and lays its real limits out plainly rather than hiding them.

 The manufacturer claims one hour at maximum power (300W). In practice, reaching 80% in 40 minutes lines up with that claim, but a full charge actually takes closer to 82 minutes, with the final stretch slowing down noticeably.

 It depends on the output: around 213 Wh (83%) through the AC outlet, up to 241 Wh (94%) through the 12V output, and over 90% through the USB-C port.

 The Allpowers Volix P300 is a compact 256 Wh portable power station, built for mobility and top-ups. It is aimed at those who want a small energy reserve easy to take camping, in a van, in remote work, or to keep at home for minor outages, without investing in a large station.
 Despite its small size and featherweight, it does not skimp on versatility: it offers a 230V mains socket (300 W continuous, up to 600 W peak), USB-C and USB-A ports to charge phones, tablets and computers, plus a 12V output. Enough to power a laptop for several recharges, a camera, a drone, a small fan or an internet box.
 Its screen clearly shows the battery level and power draw, and it recharges easily on mains, in the car or via a compatible solar panel such as the Solax SE60, to stay self-sufficient on the move. Its simple, rugged design makes it pleasant day to day.
 Keep in mind the limits of its category: with 256 Wh and 300 W, the Volix P300 is ideal for small portable devices, but not for powering large appliances or lasting long hours under heavy load. For light, mobile top-up use, it is a reliable, well-equipped companion, at a very accessible price on sale.

 Review: ALLPOWERS VOLIX P300 (300W/256Wh) Portable Power Station
 Posted on June 21, 2026 by lui_gough 
 Power stations are a product which has grown dramatically in popularity, whether it be for use on recreational trips as a power source when you are “off-grid”, or as emergency sources of power. For many years, the price has hovered at about $1/Wh for a decent quality power station, with entry level units often being 200-300Wh in capacity.
 Thanks to some very attentive OzBargainers, combined with various cashback and sale offers, the ALLPOWERS VOLIX P300 which is a 256Wh power station was on sale for just AU$145.76 and later, AU$116.72 making it an effective $0.569/Wh and $0.456/Wh without taking into account the cashback offers available at the time which would have paid back a further 15% or so.
 As a bit of a self-confessed power station aficionado, I decided to grab two units while I could, just to see if they were any good.
 Unboxing 
 These units arrive in a cardboard box with black printed line-art of the product on the front side. ALLPOWERS is not a brand that seems to achieve universal recognition online – apparently reading some of their reviews suggests their prior products were not all trouble-free. That being said, this is one of their later releases – the name “VOLIX” seems almost deliberate, sharing some similarities with “VoltX” and Anker’s “Solix” brand.  It’s Panaphonics all over again! 
 On the side, the specifications include a 256Wh (12.8V/20Ah) LFP battery, a weight of 3.57kg (approx), an 11-30V 8A 110W maximum solar input, 300W (600W surge) inverter output, 100W Max USB-C output, 18W Max USB-A output (x2) and a 12V 10A car accessory port, with a 300W combined output power limit. The unit is Made in China and while it doesn’t state it on the product, the website seems to indicate a five-year warranty although online reviews suggest that support from the company is poor.
 This particular unit was shipped from a local warehouse due to dangerous goods regulations and is an Australian plug type unit.
 Inside, the unit is safely suspended by foam blocks at both ends.
 The inclusions are  spartan – you get the unit, a mains IEC charging cable, a manual and a safety card. That’s it. If you intend to use the solar input, you’re on your own to source a compatible cable. Thankfully, the XT60 plug it uses is very common nowadays.
 The front of the unit bears some resemblance to the Ecoflow River 2/3, having the two-tone appearance and rounded rectangular design. Three buttons form the user interface – the power button, a DC output and an AC output button. Interestingly, the AC socket is rotated 90 degrees clockwise, which is  not a bad idea all things considered. It means that “tall” plug packs won’t hit the ground – instead, it would simply obscure the display instead.
 The 12V DC cigarette lighter style socket is located behind a protective rubber cover.
 Aside from that, the unit is rounded and enclosed around the rear.
 The right side of the unit has the charging inputs, consisting of an IEC socket and an XT60 socket for solar input. Cooling exhausts out of the left side through a fan grille. A carry handle folds flat into the unit’s footprint, allowing units to be stacked. This handle is arguably nicer than the “jutting-out” handle of the RIVER 2 and the integrated into the body type on the AC2A .
 The fan appears to be a USTF501512HW from Descofan.
 The top of the unit has a nice matte/gloss cross pattern with the brand subtly occupying the front lip of the top cover.
 Four round rubber feet keep it planted on a flat surface, with the product information label on the underside.
 The same specifications are shown on the unit itself.
 The included mains cable for the Australian market comes from Unirise with UE-331 GPO plug and UE-313 IEC plug.
 I did not spot any RCM logo on the plugs, but they do carry an N-number, which would have been a state-based electrical safety approval.
 The cable is 0.75mm^2 in cross-sectional area, good for at least 7.5A and up to 10A (although best not continuously).
 The included safety card was worth including because it seems to come from good intentions, but is executed in a classically Chinese way – that copy-pasted text in the bottom especially makes little sense – the first dot-point on the right says “unt[sic] of smoke during the operation of the device.”
 One interesting thing mentioned in the manual is the  4,000 cycle rating which you will see advertised on the product listings. This seems to be a bit of a case of  stretching the numbers as this is the 70% point. Many others may only state 3,000 cycles but that might be to 80% point instead. This makes it hard to definitively say which battery is better.
 User Experience 
 As I have both several Ecoflow RIVER 2 units and a Bluetti AC2A , both of which are “small” power stations of a similar capacity class, I had some good quality units to reference in my comparison.
 The first would just be size and weight. I found the unit rather comfortable to carry – the handle is the best of the three and the weight of 3587g (measured) was similar to the others. The unit was also pretty straightforward to use with the standard conventions of long-pressing the on/off button to turn on and off, and enabling each output with a short-press of the corresponding output button.
 The display makes good sense as well, although it always appeared somewhat hazy and not as sharp as it could be likely due to the glare on the cover plastic. The push buttons are a bit hollow-feeling tactile push buttons. My main gripe is that turning the station off is “ambiguous” as sometimes you do get button bounce and a short press of the power button toggles the display off but keeps the unit running. Sometimes this can mean that the station is running, but with the display off, when you intended to turn it off. My other units clearly indicate “OFF” in the display before they blank out.
 The power station, when being discharged, seemed to have some interesting behaviour. When discharging using the inverter, it seemed to cut-out at 5% remaining regardless – likely as a way to avoid stressing out the cells which usually have higher internal resistance towards the end. This cut-out did not seem to affect DC based discharging, which could get all the way down to empty. As a result, this does create some confusion with regards to computed figures. There did seem to be an issue with the display though, as when the battery was low, it had a habit of coming on a lot – sometimes this was caused by the load cycling on and off briefly (e.g. a charging device pausing for a cable resistance check), other times, it seems because the battery had ticked down in capacity remaining. The issue is that turning the screen on when the battery is low is making a bad situation worse as it is consuming what little precious energy remains.
 The 300W rating of the inverter is very normal for small power stations of this size, so you should be somewhat reasonable about what you expect it to power. For example, a beefy gaming desktop PC? Probably not – in fact, the inrush will possibly trip the inverter as was my experience trying the exact same thing. But other units of the small 300W power class couldn’t do it either, so this is not an issue for the P300 as such – just a reality that owners will have to face. It is best used with smaller appliances as a result – but the range of appliances it can be used with is a little more limited than some other power stations which have power lifting or X-BOOST style capabilities which operate the inverter at continuous power (sacrificing voltage stability) so simple appliances like heating elements can continue to work at the 300W level rather than having nothing at all. Unfortunately, the P300 does not seem to have this capability. It is also noted that, similar to some other power stations, turning on the AC output results in the output “ramping” up rather than coming on at full voltage.
 Unfortunately, when it came to connectivity, while the unit features Bluetooth, it has to be manually turned-on at each power-up of the power station by long-pressing the DC enable button without the possibility for it to come on automatically. This makes using it with the app less convenient than it could be. It also does not seem to have any security when it is on – as any app can just connect and take control of the power station in a similar way to my Bluetti AC2A.
 This unit also seems to have an ALLPOWERS trait of throwing error codes  a lot of the time . For example, after the battery is charged by mains, soon after, I discharged it a tiny bit and attempted to recharge it again and I got an E209. Other times, charging from solar, I managed an E302. In the manual, there is a list of error codes (as below):
 E209 is unfortunately not listed, but E302 for example, is not a real error. Solar input undervoltage can happen just simply because the sun is setting today – but it does mean that the unit seems to latch an error and refuses to charge on the following day. Instead, it requires you to manually wait until the sun is up, disconnect the panel, reboot the unit and plug it back in to initiate charging again. This is rather frustrating, as such errors should be automatically-clearing (or not treated as errors at all).
 Acoustically, the P300 doesn’t have all that much going for it either. I found the fan on my first unit to be even whinier and buzzier than the one on my RIVER 2, while the second unit was around the same level. It is acoustically conspicuous in a room, especially because the fan likes to cycle on and off, with some level of speed regulation, but not enough to be a smooth transition or settling on a continuous speed. When outputting AC, there was a little bit of switching converter noise audible as a hissy-buzz depending on the load, but it was relatively quiet compared to the fan. Most annoyingly, however, is setting it to “mute” mode through the app still resulted in the fan coming up occasionally.
 ALLPOWERS App 
 To get the most out of the VOLIX P300, you will need the ALLPOWERS app. During the course of the review, an update to the app fixed a bug where the device needed to be reconnected manually each time, which was nice, but even then I would have to describe the app as being pretty basic.
 You need to enable Bluetooth on your phone and on the device, scan for the power station and connect to it.
 Once connected, you can see the state of charge, estimated time remaining, input and output powers and toggle the output and frequency settings.
 The settings page allows you to control the “working mode” which is similar to Bluetti’s Turbo/Normal/Quiet modes. It also similarly has an ECO mode, which similarly, shuts down the unit after a time without load. The device can also be renamed.
 The localisation does fall apart somewhat with Mute Mode, Standard Mode and Fast Mode being the selections. The time for ECO mode shutdown can be set from a list of pre-configured values but the threshold for ECO mode and the outputs to which they apply is not configurable.
 While there is a firmware update option, it seems to be locked behind a code and this isn’t publicly available. I did try the codes that others have claimed to be the “default” but none of them were accepted.
 You can sign-up for an account but it doesn’t seem to make a difference to how the app works. Best not to use it with an account if you don’t have to.
 The last device is remembered for a quick connection from the home screen. To open another device, you need to click on the Bluetooth icon to scan again. Unfortunately, while the recent update of the app allowed it to remember the last connected device, it doesn’t remember more than one device. As a result, if you have two units (as I do), then you’ll be left manually reconnecting to the other unit each and every time.
 Test Results 
 This section features the results of certain tests and measurements made on the P300.
 USB Output Modes 
 The USB outputs were tested using the Fnirsi FNB58 to determine which modes they supported.
 The USB-C output scores well, indicating support for 105W maximum output with six PDOs in total. It indicates support for 12V output, which is not universal, along with PPS.
 The USB-A outputs support the above – unfortunately, no QC 3.0 support, but at least QC 2.0 is there and likely how the 18W maximum comes about.
 Discharge Capacity 
 Discharge capacity was tested using the Tektronix PA1000 Power Analyser.
 Testing with a 150W (nominal) halogen bulb with two units gave surprisingly similar results, however, the second unit seems to have reduced its output voltage as the battery ran low. As the discharge ends at 5% indicated capacity remaining, it suggests the inverter discharge efficiency is about 83%.
 Plotting the voltage data shows the output voltage is very stable at the 230V nominal, but with the exception of Unit 2 as it gets towards the end of its discharge. I wonder if the two units I have are running different firmware.
 A new test case is to see what happens when using a  worst case light load – in this case, a ~2.8W LED light bulb. The unit managed 15h 24m 35s of runtime, supplying just 44.58Wh to the light bulb, with the remainder lost to self-consumption. The estimated self-consumption with the AC output on is about 11.66W when servicing a very light load. This does mean that you probably wouldn’t be using this power station to run a very light AC load for a long period (e.g. the 21 hours between charges on the SSO).
 DC Discharge is a lot more efficient – in fact, the DC output shows a classic LFP discharge curve as it is just passing the internal battery to the outside world. A small amount of loss is due to the internal display circuitry and some losses in connectors and cables – but this was done to my B&K Precision Model 8600 DC Electronic Load in 4-wire mode, so cable losses are compensated for. The unit cuts output at 10.76V, for a full discharge, achieving 94.41% of the claimed energy capacity. In terms of colombic efficiency, we managed 19.67Ah of the claimed 20Ah, indicating an honest battery capacity.
 USB-C output was tested at 60W to reduce uncertainties due to eMarker cable consumption. The result is quite good – achieving over 90% discharge efficiency. It would seem this unit is best suited to running DC loads as a result.
 Charging Efficiency 
 In terms of AC charging, it seems that charging in the slowest “mute mode” is least efficient, likely as the fan still runs in mute mode and the longer charging time creates higher losses in cooling. Charging in standard and fast mode is very similar – the charging efficiency is likely in the order of 83%, considering that when discharging in AC, only 95% of the capacity is available. Therefore, the AC-to-AC round-trip efficiency is about 69%.
 Charging from the PV input provoked an undervoltage error at 11V and an overvoltage error at 30V, both of which are in the claimed supported voltage range. Nevertheless, testing was performed at 12V and 28V. At 12V, charging took 4h27m35s, while 28V took just 3h 9m 24s. The DC charging efficiency is about 87-88%. Charging at 12V is quite limited in terms of power – peaking at 68W; while at 28V, it peaked at 108W. This is a very common behaviour for MPPT inputs due to maximum current limits.
 Thermals 
 Thermals were checked using the Thermal Master P3 USB-C thermal camera .
 During charging from mains, the left side of the unit was warmest.
 The highest temperature was seen through the fan grille reaching 39 degrees C, which is acceptable for someone touching the unit from the outside. The components inside would be warmer, however.
 The temperature pattern was a little different when under a 150W AC load, with the hot spot shifting more towards the rear left.
 The maximum temperature measured was just shy of 43 degrees Celsius.
 Standby Power 
 Standby power consumption was measured using a Tektronix PA1000 Power Analyser and PWRVIEW software.
 When plugged in and charging has completed, it consumes around 3W from the wall with no outputs turned on.
 In UPS mode with pass-through of power from input to output, the consumption rises to 5W.
 AC Output Waveform 
 The AC output waveforms and changeover times are measured with a Rohde & Schwarz MXO4 oscilloscope and an HVP-70 High Voltage Differential Probe .
 The output is a “pure” sine wave in shape, although there is a little ringing around the zero voltage region.
 This persists even when under a 150W halogen light load.
 Looking in the frequency domain, the highest harmonic is about 47.4dB below the fundamental.
 Under 150W load, the highest harmonic is now 42.9dB below the fundamental, indicating a bit more harmonic noise when under load (not unusual). Nevertheless, the output waveform maintains a sinusoidal shape with a good crest factor. The only  real point of concern is that the 50Hz from the unit is consistently low at 49.92Hz (0.16% slow).
 UPS Changeover Time 
 Changeover from inverter back to mains occurs in about 16ms – this is slower than the claimed <10ms.
 Similarly, going from mains to inverter takes 16ms as well (which is also longer than the <10ms claimed), but the inverter output starts low and flat-topped, as if a square-ish wave, because the DC link bus capacitors are likely not fully charged at that point. So it would seem your load not only needs to ensure a short interruption, but also, slightly dirty power for a handful of cycles before the inverter gets into its rhythm.
 Conclusion 
 The ALLPOWERS VOLIX P300 is perhaps the cheapest small power station on the market, especially when it is on sale. In spite of this, it is a functional package in the sense that it delivers what is promised in terms of its output capabilities and capacity. It does have a slightly ambiguous warranty situation, with five years claimed by the official site but nothing indicated on reseller’s webpages or in the included documentation, with some reviews indicating issues with the company’s customer support.
 While the design of the unit overall is good in terms of layout and handle, the app and remote connectivity is not quite as polished as more premium brands with a very basic app and a Bluetooth connection that needs to be manually enabled at every power station power-up. Firmware updates are not available without a special code. Acoustically, it is more whiny and rattly than my other units and the fan noticeably cuts in and out. It’s also not quite as capable in terms of appliance compatibility due to inverter output power as it doesn’t have “power lifting” style constant-power modes to allow larger basic appliances to operate at reduced power. It also had tendencies to detect errors that would require manual intervention to restore charging or discharging especially from PV, that make it more difficult to use unattended.
 Efficiency figures were fairly decent at 83% AC discharge under 150W load, 83% AC charging in fast mode, 90% USB-C discharge at 60W, 94% 12V DC Output discharge at 10A. This gives a round-trip AC-to-AC efficiency of about 69%. Standby power consumption was about 3W, or 5W in UPS mode. While UPS changeover did not occur in <10ms as claimed, it was around 16ms measured which is still sufficiently fast for the majority of devices but with the mains-to-inverter changeover resulting in some dirty square-ish wave power as the DC bus capacitors charged up under load (i.e. poor voltage stability).
 I suppose, given the price and positioning of the unit, we can’t expect it to be a perfect match for premium-level units. So while it does “do the job” if you’re using it interactively, it might not be the unit to choose if you expect good remote control capabilities or for it to just run on PV solar without encountering errors or needing manual intervention to persuade it to charge or if you simply demand quiet operation.
 As the Solar Sharer Offer is coming soon, I’ve made some substantial investments into power stations in the hopes of making the most of the scheme, so stay tuned for more power station reviews! Just as I used to review power banks, now my site will also be the home of power station reviews.

 Best Solar Generator for Beginners 2026:
 Where to Start 
 Your first solar generator shouldn't be complicated. Here are 5 beginner-friendly picks, a plain-English guide to every spec that matters, and a decision framework that gets you to the right unit in 5 minutes.
 By S.E.T. Editorial Team 
 Published August 8, 2026 
 🕑 16 min read 
 Quick Answer: The best solar generator for beginners in 2026 is the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus ($299) . It weighs 8.4 lbs, delivers 286Wh of LiFePO4 capacity and 600W output, charges from a wall outlet in under an hour, and has the best app in the industry. All five picks below use LiFePO4 batteries (3,000+ cycle life), cost under $500, and work straight out of the box — plug in, charge, done. No solar panels required to start.
 Solar Generator Specs — Plain English
 If spec sheets make your eyes glaze over, this section is for you. Every number below gets used the same way across every brand, every model. Learn these four things and you'll never be confused by a product listing again.
 📚 The Only 4 Specs That Matter
 Capacity (Wh = watt-hours) 
 How much total energy the battery stores. Think of it as the size of the gas tank. A 300Wh battery can deliver 300 watts for 1 hour, or 100 watts for 3 hours, or 50 watts for 6 hours. Bigger number = longer runtime. 
 Output (W = watts) 
 How much power the unit can deliver at any given moment. Think of it as the size of the engine. A 600W output means you can run any combination of devices that adds up to 600W or less at the same time. This determines what you can power. A phone charger is ~20W. A laptop is ~60W. A mini-fridge is ~60-100W. A full-size fridge is ~150W. A microwave is ~1,000W. 
 Solar Input (W) 
 The maximum wattage the unit can accept from solar panels. Higher = faster solar recharging. A 200W solar input paired with a 200W panel refills a 300Wh battery in about 1.5 hours of strong sun. Solar panels are optional — every unit also charges from a wall outlet. 
 Battery Chemistry (LiFePO4 vs. NMC) 
 LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) is the modern standard. 3,000-4,000 charge cycles, safer in heat, lasts 8-10+ years. NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) is the old standard. 500-800 cycles, degrades faster. Every pick in this guide uses LiFePO4. If a generator you're looking at uses NMC in 2026, skip it. 
 That's it. Capacity tells you how long. Output tells you what. Solar input tells you how fast you recharge off-grid. Battery chemistry tells you how long the unit itself lasts. Everything else — surge watts, X-Boost mode, pass-through charging — is a nice-to-have, not a dealbreaker for your first unit. For the full deep dive, see our sizing guide .
